title: Data Staged: Local Data Staging
summary: Local data staging keeps the collected material on the machine where it was found, which makes it the quietest form of consolidation because no network traffic is generated until the very end. The parent technique describes gathering data centrally before exfiltration; this sub-technique is the same pattern confined to one host. After searching the file system, a mail client cache, or a database, the attacker copies or moves the selected files into a single directory, often a temporary path, a user profile folder, or a directory that already contains many files of the same kind, and may compress the result into one archive with a standard tool. Some variants avoid files altogether and store data inside a local database, application store, or the Windows Registry, where a small amount is easy to hide and even easier to overlook. Detection depends on volume and context rather than on any one operation, because copying and compressing files are ordinary user actions. Successive file reads from unrelated directories by a single process, a new directory or archive whose contents came from many locations, archive utilities or scripting interpreters launched by an unusual parent, writes to temporary or hidden paths that end in a large outbound connection, and a sudden increase in disk usage on a workstation are the kinds of evidence that separate staging from routine work.

beginner.definition: Local data staging means gathering stolen files in one place on the same computer. The attacker copies the files into a single folder or archive. Later they send that one collection out of the network.
beginner.whyItMatters: This happens before the data leaves, so it is your last clear chance to notice the theft. Finding the folder tells you exactly which documents mattered and how much was taken.
howItWorks: The attacker searches a computer for valuable files, such as documents, keys, or saved passwords.
They copy those files into one folder instead of leaving them where they were found.
Often they use a standard tool to pack the files into a single file that is smaller and easier to send.
The folder is often a temporary path or a user profile folder that people rarely inspect.
Sometimes they store the data inside a database or a system settings store instead of a normal file.
When everything is ready, they send the collection out in one transfer and may delete the folder.
beginner.example: A thief spends the night in an office. Instead of carrying one item out at a time, they collect laptops, keys, and papers from every desk and pile them in a storage cupboard. Then they empty the cupboard in one trip.
takeaways: Local staging creates no network traffic, so endpoint monitoring is the only way to see it.
A folder receiving files from many different locations is more telling than the copy itself.
Check for archives created by scripting tools in temporary and user profile directories.

objectives: Explain how local data staging differs from the parent data staging technique.
List the local locations attackers commonly use to hold collected data.
Describe how compression tools and archives appear in endpoint telemetry.
Explain why staging inside a database or registry is hard to spot.
Describe the file read and write patterns that indicate collection on one host.
